Every screen · batches 1–27

The Covenant Wedding Planner

Fifty-one screens covering all thirty-seven pages of the planner, newest batch first. Every one is the same frame — top bar, tabs, sub-nav, 224px rail, page header with a single primary action, stat strip, toolbar, bulk bar, work surface, 360px drawer — because a page that invents its own shape costs the user the thing they had already learned. Where a page needed something the system did not have, it borrowed an existing part rather than inventing one: the nested child-record panel from §13 carries contract instalments and counseling homework alike.

Two files sit beside this one. Covenant Design Spec is the system these were drawn from — tokens, page anatomy, table rules, print classes, and the record of every deliberate divergence from the existing app. Planner Prototype is the wiring underneath: six of these pages built as working software on one shared store, where declining a guest really does empty a seat, move a headcount and re-derive a budget line. These screens are drawings of state; that file proves the state is real.

Batch 27 · drawer tabs · Documents, and the last five

The last thirty-eight tabs

Note, packet, template, printable, hub table, hub row, essentials item, name-change step, history entry and setup field — the ten record types that were still first-tab-only. With this batch every drawer tab in the planner is drawn.

Four of these ten are about the planner, not the wedding

Hub table, hub row, history entry and setup field describe the software itself. Their tabs answer developer questions — what are the real field names, what does undo actually restore, what breaks if I change this — and they are the only drawers that show raw JSON or a snapshot position.

A valid link to an incomplete thing

The hub row’s Links tab distinguishes two different failures: a link pointing at a deleted table, and a link pointing at a menu item that exists but has no dish. Six of the first, one of the second, and conflating them would send you to the wrong page.

The checklist that is truthful and wrong

The marriage licence is marked “in the bag” and has not been collected — the status describes the folder, not the document. Its note contradicts itself about the collection date and nobody has fixed it. Both are drawn as they are, because that is the state.

Printing and sending are logged, because paper goes stale

The day-of timeline was printed on 26 July and the timeline has changed twice since, so the copy in someone’s folder is wrong. The template log shows 26 sends and 31 still pending — evidence that chasing by email has stopped working.

Batch 26 · drawer tabs · Covenant

Four records where the prose is the point

Vision section, prayer entry, counseling session and rhythm — from 13a, 13b, 13c and 13d. These are the Class B records, and they break two habits the other twenty do not.

Prose is the record, not a note about it

Everywhere else a text field is a note beside the data. Here the wording is the data, so it renders in Cormorant inside the 360px drawer — because it will print in Cormorant, and a keepsake edited in the wrong face gets written in the wrong voice.

Print is a tab here and nowhere else

For every other record printing is a by-product. For a Covenant record the printed page is the deliverable, so the drawer shows the page proof and logs each print — an edited keepsake means the paper copy in the drawer at home is now wrong.

Status is derived from the prose

A prayer is answered when an answer exists — there is no tick. A session is complete when its homework rows are, not when someone says so. Both refuse the separate flag that could disagree with the thing it describes.

The one record that cannot be shared

Prayer is greyed out in the share-packet picker rather than hidden, so you can see it was withheld on purpose. Privacy belongs to the record type, which is why that tab shows facts instead of toggles.

Batch 25 · drawer tabs · The Day

Five records that all owe a minute

Ceremony element, movement, appointment, booking and day event — from 11a, 11d, 14a, 17b and 6b. Every one of these five has a duration, and in four of them a single edited minute moves something else.

Duration is the input; time is the output

Editing the vows from 5 to 6 minutes pushed five later elements and took the ceremony from 51 to 52. Adding five minutes to the ceremony block moved the whole evening. Start times are consequences, so the drawer never lets you type one directly.

Three tabs exist to hold a clash

Travel: moving the tasting one hour turned ninety minutes of slack into minus fifteen. Transport: three runs, one driver who leaves at 5pm. Run sheet: cue 1 depends on a sound operator nobody has contracted.

The planner did not warn, and says so

Today’s Lagos pair created the driver clash, because the conflict is between a movement and an appointment and nothing checks across the two. Stating the gap is better than implying a check that does not run.

The honeymoon is real money in no total

$1,840 non-refundable, 44% of the committed trip budget, tied to a wedding date that would cost $240 to move. It appears in no wedding figure — deliberate, but the Cost tab refuses to let that read as free.

Batch 24 · drawer tabs · Vendors

Four vendor records, sixteen tabs

Menu item, song, shot and vision pin — from 7a, 10d, 11b and 8b. What these four share is that each one has a tab whose whole job is to say what will go wrong.

One record here cannot be costed

The vegetarian main has nine guests and no dish, so it contributes nothing to the $8,938 catering total — meaning the true figure is higher than the page can show. The Costing tab states that and offers an estimate it refuses to add in.

Derived counts are not editable

The nine vegetarians come from nine guest records. The Guests tab lists them read-only and says why: a guest changing their meal changes this count, so typing over it would be a lie that lasts until the next RSVP.

A shared thing cannot be unshared

Once a pin goes to Bloom Studio the vendor has it. The History tab says changing it afterwards means telling them, rather than pretending the link is live — and the Colours tab catches the off-palette brass before it becomes the wedding’s colour by accident.

The tab that holds the real risk

Timing: fourteen formals in twelve minutes is fifty-one seconds each. Performer: an unamplified kora in a room nobody has sound-checked. Neither is visible from the table — both are one tab deep.

Batch 23 · drawer tabs · People

Five people records, twenty-one tabs

Wedding party, table, gift, household and contact — every figure read from 10a, 8a, 10b, 14b and 14c.

Three of these five are not records

Household and Contact are projections — a household groups guest records, a contact is a guest or vendor seen through one lens. Each says so in its first tab, because a drawer that looks like a record but writes somewhere else is the most expensive kind of surprise.

A party member is a guest first

Name, side and table live on the guest record. 10a adds only role, attire, duties and fitting — and its History tab covers only those four, with everything else logged on the guest.

The Seats tab suggests, it does not decide

It offers Efua for T4’s free seat because she is in the same household and unseated. A suggestion derived from two fields is worth more than an empty slot, and it names its reasoning.

Capacity refuses rather than displaces

Reducing T4 below its seated count names who it would unseat instead of silently dropping them. The 26 July change from 10 to 8 is why two of the 24 unseated guests exist, and History still says so.

Batch 22 · drawer tabs · Money

Two money records, eight tabs

Every drawer in the planner shows its tab strip, but until now only the first tab was drawn. This batch works through them a category at a time, starting with Money — the budget line item from 4a and the contract from 10c. Every figure is read from those two screens, not invented.

Money records tab by who is owed and when

A budget line splits into the line, its category, its payment and its history. Not into “details / more details” — each tab answers a question someone actually asks: what does it cost, what allowance does it eat, who is paying it, and who changed it.

The variance lives on the category

A line item can go over estimate; only the category can be over budget. So the $85 variance is stated on the Line item tab and carried on the Category tab, and the History tab shows that both moved in one edit.

A missing thing is a stated thing

The line item has no contract behind its $265. The contract has no payment schedule and two documents outstanding. All three are drawn as warnings inside the tab that owns them, rather than left for a reconciliation later.

Only a contract total is authoritative

Editing it re-derives the Budget row, the outstanding balance and the Dashboard percentage — so that one edit confirms first. A line-item actual does not: it is already the lowest level.

Batch 21 · the Guest List, in full

Three views of 142 people

The guest record is the largest in the planner — twenty-four fields — and eight other pages read from it. So the page needs three views and the record needs seven tabs, and the interesting question in every case is what gets left out. Six columns of twenty-four in the table, because the name column has a floor. Envelopes instead of people in Households, because that is what invitations go to. A queue instead of a room in Seating, because Table Layout already owns the room.

Why RSVP is per event

The 130 invited to the ceremony are not the 22 invited to the rehearsal dinner. One RSVP field on the guest record would have to mean one of them and silently lose the rest.

The brunch has not gone out

Thirty-four invited, nothing back — because the invitation has not been sent. Invite decision made, Invite sent blank: the two fields the drawer keeps apart.

What the headcount uses

Catering derives from reception acceptances only. The rehearsal dinner is a separate 22-cover job on Weekend Logistics, and the brunch is not catered at all yet.

The eighteen columns that are not here
Hidden by the column budget, not by accident
Open the full editor
Why six

The name column has a 240px floor. After the rail and the drawer, six columns is what fits without squeezing names — so the six are the ones you scan by: who, whose household, which side, replied, seated, fed.

Where the rest live

Address, phone, email, dietary detail, plus-one, gift, thank-you, invitation dates and the notes all sit in the record editor. Nothing is lost; it is one click, not one scroll.

What the Columns chip does

It says 6 of 24 and lets you swap any of them in. It does not widen the table — a seventh column takes a sixth away.

What this view is for
Three things the flat list answers badly
Open Table view
One envelope, one row

Invitations, save-the-dates and thank-you letters go to a household, not a person. 142 guests are 62 envelopes, and this is the only view that says so.

Split households show up

The Mensah household sits across T1 and T14 because two of its four are children. Amber, not red — sometimes that is deliberate, and the view states it rather than judging it.

This is a view, not a page

It groups guest records; it owns nothing. Editing a name here edits the guest. The separate Households page in the sub-nav is a different thing — it adds fields an envelope needs that a guest does not.

Why the columns are status and not phase
The one decision that makes a board worth having
Open Table view
Phase is already two other things

Phases are ordered and dated, so they are a timeline — the rail carries them and so does the Timeline view. As columns they would give three views of one axis and none of status.

Status is what you drag

A board earns its place when moving a card means something. Dragging changes status, a field you touch constantly; phase is set once when the task is written.

Blocked is a column, not a note

It is not a stage between in-progress and complete — it is a stop. Two cards in a red column reads differently from two amber cards with a footnote, and both of these are also the page’s two overdue tasks.

Three groupings, not one

Household is the envelope. Family is the bloodline the seating chart respects — cousins who should sit together across two households. Group is why they were invited. Collapsing any two of them loses a real question the couple asks.

Invite decision is not RSVP

The first is the couple’s choice, the second is the guest’s. Twelve guests are decided but unsent, which is why the rail counts “Not invited yet” separately from “Pending”.

+1 and Kids live with Response

Not with Invitation, though that is where they are decided — because each one adds a cover to the catering headcount, and Response is the tab that owns what this record costs to feed.

Role and Side moved off the Party tab

Every guest has both, and Party is conditional — ten of 142 see it. A field on a conditional tab is a field 132 people cannot reach.

Identity
Name and the four groupings — Household, Family, Group, Side — plus Role. All five are separate fields and the tab says why.

Batch 20 · the two views 14a promised

Calendar and Agenda

14a’s switcher offers Table, Calendar and Agenda; only Table was drawn. These are the other two. Both had to earn their place against the Smart Calendar, which already has month, week and agenda — and the answer is travel. Smart Calendar carries eighty-three entries from five sources and most of them have no travel field, so it cannot draw one. These nine do, which is why the clash is visible here and nowhere else.

The three views divide cleanly by what you are doing: Table edits, Calendar reasons about time, Agenda reads and prints. Same records throughout — which is why they are a view switcher and not tabs, per §07b test 03.

20a
Appointments · Calendar view
The two views 14a names in its switcher but never draws. Same nine records, drawn on time. A month grid would be ninety per cent empty, so this is a two-week time grid with empty days collapsed — and travel is a hatched band before each block: one journey, one band, drawn only on the arrival side so the trip between two appointments is never counted twice. On 20 August the blocks never touch, but the 75-minute run from Adenta overlaps the tasting by fifteen minutes. That red sliver is the clash.

What this view drops, and why
Three things the table has that an agenda must not
Open Table view
No checkboxes

Selection belongs to the Table view. A column of empty boxes down the left of a reading document invites a click that does nothing useful here.

No column controls

There are no columns, so Auto-fit and Row height have nothing to act on. The toolbar keeps the three filters and the switcher, and drops the rest.

No drawer

Clicking a line returns you to Table view with that row open, rather than sliding a panel over the document you are reading.

Batch 18 · the last two

Homecoming & History

Both are tables, per your call. Newlywed Homecoming runs three of them — settling in, an eleven-institution name-change tracker where order genuinely matters, and a first month of money that is deliberately not part of the $30,000 — then allows itself one reflective section at the very end. Planner History is the first page in the system with no tab: it is reached from the undo and redo buttons, so nothing is lit and the sub-nav says so. Rows expand to field-level diffs, and a row can only be undone while its snapshot is one of the fifteen still kept — which is why the older ones read “snapshot aged out” rather than offering a button that would fail.

Why some rows cannot be undone
Two different things are kept, and they run out at different speeds
Read about backups
The log · 250 entries

A readable line per change, with the fields that moved. Cheap to keep, so it goes back to 2 June.

214 kept · 86% full
Snapshots · 15

A full copy of the planner before each change. Expensive, so only the last fifteen survive — which is why undo runs out long before the log does.

Neither is a backup

Both live in this browser and both go if the site data is cleared. A .sqlite backup is the only thing that survives that.

Batch 17 · from the audit

Two pages I had missed

The Essentials Checklist is the page whose name I took for the setup page — it is the physical packing list, and its only real status is whether a thing is in a bag. Honeymoon & After was a whole nav group that never entered the inventory; it runs seven sections behind a tab bar and is the only page that begins after the wedding. Its two after-the-day counts are read from Gifts and Tasks rather than typed, which is what keeps “4 notes due” honest. Two pages remain undrawn: Newlywed Homecoming and Planner History.

17aEssentials Checklist17bHoneymoon & After
17a
Essentials Checklist
Not a settings page — the thing you physically pack. Every row is an object that must be in a named bag, held by a named person, in a named place, and the only status that matters on the morning is whether it is in the bag. Distinct from Wedding Setup, which is why the naming collision had to be resolved.

Batch 16 · global chrome

Viewer preferences

The first piece of chrome rather than a page. It hangs off the avatar already in the top bar — not a new gear beside it, which would put two settings affordances within 30px of each other. One rule decides what goes in: a setting belongs here only if it changes what you see and nothing a share-packet recipient would ever receive. Everything that fails that test stays on Wedding Setup.

16aViewer preferences
16a
Viewer preferences · the avatar menu
Undo and redo now sit in the top bar on every screen — the second piece of always-present chrome, and the reason this menu carries only a shortcut reminder rather than the controls themselves. No gear icon — the avatar already sits top-right and clicking it opens this, so there is one affordance rather than two side by side. Everything inside changes what you see; nothing in it changes a record, a total, or anything a share-packet recipient would receive. That is the test for whether a setting belongs here or on Wedding Setup.

Batch 15 · Start Planning

The four pages I dropped

Wedding Setup, Get Started, Page-by-Page Guide and FAQ — the app’s Start Planning group, which I removed from §06 when I replaced its sub-nav. Wedding Setup is restored to its own name; the page I had called Essentials was always this, and Essentials Checklist is a different page about buying things. The other three are reference pages: same shell, same rail, same page header, but the work surface carries prose, the rail becomes a table of contents, and there is no stat strip, toolbar, bulk bar or drawer — because there is no record open. Overview’s sub-nav now reads Dashboard · Get Started · Page-by-Page Guide · FAQ · Wedding Setup · Notes.

Get Started

Open the guide
Print section
Full editor
Print this page
Download backup

This planner runs entirely on your own computer. Everything you type saves automatically to a private database in this browser. Nothing is uploaded, and nothing is kept anywhere else unless you download a backup yourself.

That is the whole promise of the product, and it is also the one risk. Read the next box before you type anything you would be upset to lose.

Read this first

If you clear your browser history, cookies or site data — or open the planner on another device without restoring a backup — your saved work will not be there.

Wait a few seconds after opening the planner before your first backup, so the database finishes loading.

Download backupRestore

Editing & navigation
How to use the planner like a workbook
Two ways to edit a record

Click a row to open the side drawer for a quick change, or Full editor for all the fields at once. Both write to the same record.

Tables edit in place

Type in a cell, tick rows for bulk edits, and use the last row to add. Long text wraps and can be dragged taller.

Focus when it feels big

Profile & Display → Focus on essentials hides advanced pages without deleting anything. Wedding Setup has the full list.

Undo, redo and the change log

Undo and redo cover the last 15 changes. Planner History keeps a day-by-day log of what changed — it is view-only, so it tells you what happened without offering to roll back.

Planning with your partner
No account, no cloud — three files
Open Share Packets
You
Download backup
.sqlite
Partner
Restores it
same file
Partner
Sends one back
.sqlite
You
Import packet
merges

A partner packet merges RSVP updates and new tasks — it never deletes what you already have. Use a Share Packet instead when someone only needs to read details, not edit them.

What this planner cannot do
Said plainly, so it is not discovered late
Open Email Templates
It cannot send email

No invitations, no RSVP reminders, no vendor mail. Email Templates writes the letters and you send them from your own mail app.

It cannot collect RSVPs

There is no web form. Replies are entered on the Guest List by whoever hears them.

It cannot sync between devices

Two devices means two planners. The backup file is the only bridge.

It cannot recover a cleared browser

If site data goes without a backup, the planner is gone. This is the only unrecoverable failure.

▾
Where is my planner data actually stored?
Saving

On this computer, in this browser. The planner writes to a private SQLite database with a localStorage mirror for crash safety. Nothing is uploaded and there is no account. That is why a backup file is the only way to move your planner to another device — and the only thing that survives clearing your browser data.

▸
How often should I download a backup?
Saving
▸
I opened the planner on my phone and it is empty. Why?
Saving
▾
Can the planner send my invitations or RSVP reminders?
Sharing

No. It writes the letters and you send them yourself. Email Templates merges your guest and wedding details into ready text that you copy into your own mail app; the planner never has your mail account.

▸
How do guests RSVP?
Guests
▸
Why does my guest count differ from my seat count?
Guests

Batch 14 · closing the inventory

The last three pages

Appointments feeds the Smart Calendar and owns the one field the calendar cannot show — travel allowance, which is what turns two harmless green blocks into a real clash. Households and Contacts are derived views: they group the guest and vendor tables rather than storing anything, so both carry a read-only rule instead of an add button for the thing they are named after. All thirty-one pages in the inventory are now drawn.

No household records exist

An address edit fans out

Counts cannot be typed

“4 of 4 replied” is counted from the guests, so this page and the Guest List can never disagree.

The four pages a couple keeps

The frame does not change — same rail, same header, same drawer — but the work surface is set to be read rather than scanned, because these are the Class B pages. Our vision

We are building a home where the door is always heavier on the way out than on the way in — a place people arrive tired and leave fed, and where the two of us are more honest with each other than with anyone else alive.

We want a marriage that is unremarkable from the outside and extraordinary from the inside. Not a performance of a good marriage, but the slow, ordinary work of one: showing up, telling the truth early, forgiving quickly, and praying together even on the nights when neither of us feels like it.

Our values · 5
Named by both of us, in the order we argued them into place
Reorder
01
Honesty first

We tell each other the hard thing within a day, not a week. A delayed truth is a lie with better manners.

02
An open table

We would rather stretch a meal for six into a meal for nine than eat well alone.

03
Money in the light

No separate accounts, no secret spending, no purchase either of us would hide.

04
Rest is obedience

We keep a Sabbath. The work will still be there on Monday and so will we.

05
We repair fast

We do not go to sleep on it. Not as a rule about sleep — as a rule about pride.

Promises · 6

Move to vows
Ama’s promises
01

To tell you the thing I am afraid to tell you, on the day I am afraid of it.

02

To keep a home you are glad to come back to, not one you are afraid to disturb.

03

To pray for you by name, out loud, every week of our life.

Kwesi’s promises
01

To listen all the way to the end before I answer.

02

To carry the weight I can see and ask about the weight I cannot.

03

To lead by going first, not by going ahead.

Answered30 June 2026 · Both
A house we can afford

We asked for somewhere in Adenta we could pay for without borrowing from either family. We had seen eleven and every one was either out of reach or falling down.

The answer

Answered 24 July — the Adenta flat came back on the market $400 below what we had budgeted, because the previous buyer pulled out. We move in two weeks after the wedding.

Answered12 May 2026 · Ama
That Mum would come round

She has not said a word about the wedding since March.

The answer

Answered 2 July — she asked to help choose the fabric. That was the whole answer.

Still praying18 July 2026 · Kwesi
For my father’s health before November

The consultant wants to see him again in September. He wants to walk Ama’s mother down the aisle and I want him to be able to.

Still praying21 July 2026 · Both
That we would not lose each other in the planning

We have had three arguments this month and all three were about a spreadsheet.

Laid down14 April 2026 · Ama
A December date

We wanted December. The hall had nothing until March. We stopped asking and took 8 November, and we are glad.

What we have written down
Four sessions of notes, kept as a single record and printed as a Class B keepsake
Print the record
02 · How we argue

We both retreat. Ama goes quiet and Kwesi goes busy, and we have spent four years mistaking each other’s retreat for indifference. Rev. Mensah gave us the phrase “I am not finished, I am gathering” and it has already stopped one argument.

04 · Money in the light

We came in disagreeing about the wedding budget and left disagreeing about it, but with a rule: no purchase over $200 without both of us. That rule is now the third value on our Vision page.

Batch 12 · Documents

What leaves the planner

Four pages about output. Notes catches what nothing else holds; Share Packets is built around what the recipient sees rather than what went in; Email Templates shows the resolved letter beside its merge fields; Print Centre sorts every printable into the two print classes from §09 and refuses to confuse them.

Batch 10 · People, money and the vendors who play

Four record pages

Each one is a table page with a drawer, and each one earns its place by owning fields no other page carries. Contracts introduces the §13 child panel for instalments — the same component the Payments page uses — and Entertainment is the first page whose rows are ordered by a moment on the day rather than by a date.

Batch 7 · Calendar views

Week & Agenda

The three calendar views from 6a’s switcher, so you can see all of them. Same rail, same twelve source toggles, same records — only the shape of the work surface changes. Week is honest about being sparse this far out: the chosen week holds exactly what the month grid shows for 17–23 August, which is the 20th’s overlap and the 22nd’s decision deadline. Agenda is the view that actually gets used day to day.

6c
Calendar · Week
The only view where time of day is geometry rather than a label, which is why it is the one that shows the overlap properly: the tasting and the counseling session sit side by side in the 6 pm row with the shared half-hour hatched. All-day and due-date entries can’t be placed on an hour, so they get their own band above the grid instead of being dropped at midnight.

Batch 6 · Screens in the 2a system · final pair

The room & the look

The last two screens are the ones that aren’t tables. Table Layout is a plan of the room whose numbers still reconcile to the Guest List — 118 seated, 2 free seats, 24 unseated, short by 22. Vision Board is the only page where images carry the meaning, so it gets real placeholders for you to fill rather than invented artwork.

8a
Table Layout
Fifteen tables as seat grids rather than drawn circles — a filled square is an assigned guest, so capacity is readable at a glance and the page prints. The arithmetic is the honest part: 120 seats, 118 assigned, 2 free, and 24 guests still unseated, which means the room is 22 seats short. The rail says why each of the 24 can’t be seated yet.

Batch 5 · Screens in the 2a system

Food & data

Catering is where the guest list turns into money, so it is the one page that has to show two numbers at once: what the caterer is contracted for and what the RSVPs now say. The Database Hub is the planner’s safety net — it owns backup, restore and the four linked-record problems the Dashboard reports.

7a
Catering & Menu
Owns the Food, Cake, Drinks and Rentals budget lines — which is why those rows are read-only on the Budget page. Batch 4 · Screens in the 2a system

Time

Two screens about time, one about the year and one about a single day. The calendar is the only page whose work surface is a grid rather than a table — everything above it is unchanged. Both reconcile to the same ledger: August shows the $4,200 due from Payments, and the day-of vendor calls match the Contacts sheet.

6a
Smart Calendar
Nothing is authored here — every entry is a task, payment, appointment or counseling session that already exists elsewhere, colour-coded by source and read back onto the month. That is what makes it “smart”, and it is why the rail lists sources rather than filters you have to maintain. Overlaps are detected rather than allowed: 20 August holds two 6-o’clock commitments and is flagged. The stat strip counts only the month on screen — 10 entries, 3 appointments, 3 dated tasks — while the rail counts all dates, so the two sections are labelled with their scope rather than left to be guessed.

The full editor, popped out

The 360px drawer is for quick edits — seven tabs, one group of fields at a time. The Full editor button in every page header opens the same record as a resizable window with every field visible at once, plus the linked records the drawer only summarises. Same component per record type; Budget, Payments and Vendors get their own field groups.

Batch 2 · Screens in the 2a system

Money & Vendors

Three screens that share one spine. Budget is a table of categories with a spend bar per row; Payments is the same table shape keyed to due dates and vendors; Venue & Vendors keeps the compare-cards behaviour from the current product but inside the standard frame. All money is right-aligned and tabular.

4a
Budget — full page
Every section of the current page, in reading order: stat strip → budget-used bar → Budget by Category (all six utility buttons, ranked) → category rows → Budget Reconciliation with By category / By vendor → True Total projection → Budget Logic → Tipping Etiquette → the itemized table for the selected category, built on the Guest List pattern (grouped rows, checkbox column, bulk bar, filter chips, inline add row, row drawer). Note: Budget Logic and Tipping Etiquette exist in planner.css but have no markup in today's page, and True Total only appears in the m3 dashboard mockup — so those three are new here, built to match.

Budget logic
How these numbers are produced
Planned is what you set per category — either a target percentage of the total budget or a fixed dollar amount. Percentages recalculate when the total changes; fixed amounts don't.
Spent is budget entries plus synced payments, and a category is only ever counted in one of those two columns. The moment a payment record is linked to a category, that category’s money moves wholly into Payments and its manual entries stop counting — so nothing double-counts. Photography and the Emergency fund are the only manual categories here; the other six are payment-backed.
Category owners — Catering & Menu owns Food, Cake, Drinks and Rentals; Payments owns anything with a contract. Those rows are read-only here and edited on the page that owns them.
Gratuity is the sum of the ticked Tipping Etiquette rows — $1,000. Where a vendor record already carries a gratuity (Grace Hall $250, Adom Sound $200) that is the same money, counted once here, not added twice.
Variance is planned minus spent, so negative means over target. The Emergency fund is excluded from the True Total until you spend from it.
Tipping etiquette

Customary in Ghana and the US — guidance, not obligation. Tick a row to add it to the budget as a planned gratuity.

4b
Payments
Grouped by due month so the next cash-out is always at the top. The record's gratuity fields (amount and status) get their own columns rather than hiding in notes, and the drawer shows the budget category and contract each payment is wired to. Each payment can carry an installment plan — expand a row, or use the drawer’s Installments tab. Committed here counts payment records only ($20,440); Budget’s $22,040 adds the $1,600 of manual entries with no payment record behind them.

Dashboard & Guest List

Same frame every time: tabs → sub-nav → 224px rail → page header → stat strip → toolbar → work surface. Dashboard is the one page with no table, so it swaps the work surface for a summary grid. Guest List is the densest table in the product and shows saved views, bulk edit and the row drawer under real load.

3a
Dashboard
Answers one question on load: what needs me today. Next best step gets the only primary button; alerts are a list, not badges; the day-of timeline preview and budget/RSVP health sit below. The rail carries jump links rather than saved views, because there is nothing here to filter. Carried over from today's dashboard: the live months/days/hours/minutes/seconds countdown, the three ring charts (budget, RSVP, task completion), the guided planning path, planning health, data health, and the full 18-row section progress list — all rebuilt on the 2a grid.
